A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPA study, and their supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends after its references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 supplies supplementary Sections 6-13. This material can be identified as newly supplied evidence without assuming the underlying experiments were newly performed.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation benchmarks, component ablations, clinician-alignment results, interaction-efficiency experiments and a two-participant user study.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and reports additional sensitivity, failure-rate, interaction-behavior and user-study results, including supplementary Tables 4-7.

M1.justification: The Gaussian-mixture conditioning, segmentation backbone, clustering and iterative feedback framework remain. However, v1 explicitly encodes a sampled disagreement point and uniformly initializes Gaussian parameters, whereas v2 describes selected-mask encoding and prompt-conditioned initialization. v2 Section 8 nevertheless says a representative point is sampled. These descriptions prevent confidently separating procedural changes from expanded implementation disclosure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same seven tasks from REFUGE2, LIDC-IDRI and QUBIQ, covering fundus, lung, brain, prostate and kidney segmentation. Additional analyses reuse this coverage; more participants, additional held-out annotators and carrying GMM parameters between kidney images change evaluation settings rather than the represented datasets or segmentation tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same deterministic, uncertainty-aware and interactive comparators, including both SAM-U variants. MedSAM remains the human-study comparator. Supplementary interactive comparisons use the existing comparator set; the clinician-specific U-Net experiment does not introduce another method evaluated against SPA.

E3.justification: The reported leave-one-user-out evaluation expands from one excluded clinician to three different held-out users, and the human study expands from two participants to five. New comparisons vary prediction counts and reuse user-adapted GMM parameters across images. The principal dataset splits, Dice metric, six-iteration evaluation cap and failure penalty remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 supplies substantial additional analyses: clinician-specific annotation consistency, sensitivity to 24/36/48 predictions, failure rates, results for three held-out users, candidate similarity across interactions, per-iteration prediction changes and qualitative clinician alignment. These investigate mechanisms and robustness beyond v1's available evidence. The original component ablation in Table 3 is unchanged.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly averages three distinct leave-one-user-out runs and provides individual-user results in Table 6. Figure 5 adds across-image similarity distributions as boxplots. These extend aggregation and variability reporting, but neither version provides seed-based repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 1-3 retain their numerical values, but v2 adds supplementary result tables, three additional participants' timings, sampling-sensitivity scores and a Kidney transfer comparison of 91.68% versus 92.43% Dice. Held-out-user iteration results change from 5.63/7.69 for one clinician to 3.01/5.02 averaged across three users; these are different evaluations, not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v1 asserts convergence and refers to an unavailable appendix proof. v2 Section 7 supplies a substantive derivation using component posteriors, expected log likelihoods and KL separation for Gaussian components. The addition contains mathematical problems: Equation 5 assigns the wrong sign to the expected log-likelihood difference, and Equations 6-7 use inconsistent likelihood ratios.

C1.justification: The main claims of efficient preference adaptation, reduced interaction effort and strong segmentation performance remain, including the 35%/39% headline figures. The introduction drops v1's explicit claim to be the first framework specifically designed for this alignment, describing SPA as a new framework instead.

C2.justification: The supplement adds substantive interpretations linking clinician-specific annotation patterns to learnable interaction behavior, annotation fusion to reduced individual bias, and initial candidate divergence followed by convergence to preference adaptation. It also explains point sampling as protection against overfitting. These extend v1's comparatively brief interpretations of final accuracy, alignment and component ablations.

D1.justification: v2 adds Algorithm 1, detailed GMM-generator training, encoder specifications, PyTorch version, feature dimension, per-iteration runtime and a code-access link. The supplement explains annotation-combination sampling, initial prompt selection and user-study procedures; the main text first specifies 100 study images. The existing N=48, M=16 and K=4 settings are retained rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 removes the general Medical Image Segmentation subsection and five associated background references, while adding Dehnad et al. on multiple-choice question options to justify four candidates. The core uncertainty-aware and interactive segmentation literature remains. The explicit first-framework novelty positioning is softened.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and contribution statements receive extensive editing. The methodology is substantially rewritten and reorganized: preference-distribution modeling moves from Section 3.4 to 3.1, workflow receives a separate subsection, and training presentation is replaced by expanded prose and pseudocode. Terminology is standardized around users and representative segmentation candidates.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 2 to show the distribution generator and its parameter-prediction branches, reorients examples in Figure 3, and adds Algorithm 1, Tables 4-7 and Figures 5-7. These introduce substantial new visual presentation. Figures 1 and 4 and the principal table structures remain largely unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reproducibility and support for interaction efficiency through detailed training and evaluation documentation, a five-participant study, three held-out-user evaluations and additional diagnostic analyses. However, the newly supplied convergence derivation contains sign and likelihood-ratio errors, and the main text and supplement leave feedback encoding ambiguous. The practical documentation and empirical gains support a limited overall improvement, without resolving these theoretical and methodological weaknesses.
